content.title: About
content.content: Flavored shredded wheat is a whole‑grain dry breakfast cereal made of thin wheat sheets coated with a sweet or fruit‑flavored blend. It has a crisp texture and a light sweet taste, perfect for a quick meal with milk or yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shredded wheat was introduced in the United States in the early 1920s as one of the first ready‑to‑eat cereals.
Traditionally the sheets are formed from whole wheat without added sugar; flavorings are added later.
Unlike puffed cereals, each sheet retains its shape when soaked, making it useful for breading in cooking.
Flavored versions may contain natural fruit extracts and a modest amount of sugar.

items.title: Whole‑grain source
items.content: Shredded wheat provides whole‑grain wheat, rich in dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The product contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains supply B1, B3 and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Helps blood‑sugar stability
items.content: Fiber slows carbohydrate absorption, aiding in glucose level control after meals.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The cereal contains gluten and may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Flavored varieties can contain added sugar, which should be considered by individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Possible artificial flavorings
items.content: Some versions use artificial flavors that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour hot milk, water, or yogurt over the wheat sheets and let them sit for 2–3 minutes. Add fresh berries, nuts, or honey for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed package. After opening, use within 4–6 weeks to maintain crispness.

chicken-breast-baked-broiled-or-roasted-.title: Chicken breast, baked, broiled, or roasted, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken breast is a lean source of protein obtained by baking, broiling, or roasting. The meat is tender, low in fat, and commonly used in health‑focused diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides more protein per 100 g than most other meat cuts.
When cooked without skin, the fat content drops by almost half compared with pan‑frying.
The meat is rich in vitamin B6, which plays a role in amino‑acid metabolism.
In culinary practice, breast is often marinated in lemon juice or yogurt to retain moisture.
A popular method is “en papillote” – cooking the breast in parchment with herbs to lock in flavor and juices.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: With about 31 g of protein per 100 g, it supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Skinless breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6 and niacin aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: Protein digests slowly, helping to maintain fullness longer.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Pre‑made marinades can be high in salt; monitor sodium intake if needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the breast for salads, sandwiches, stir‑fries, or serve it whole with vegetable sides. Marinating in lemon, olive oil and herbs before baking enhances juiciness and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh breast in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Freeze at –18 °C for up to 9 months. Thaw in the fridge rather than at room temperature before cooking.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-made-with-ma.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg, made with margarine (1972)

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet prepared with margarine is a simple dish that became popular in the early 1970s. Eggs are beaten, a small amount of margarine is added, and the mixture is cooked on a skillet until golden. The dish is protein‑rich, fatty, quick to make, and was often served as breakfast or a light dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In the 1970s margarine was cheaper and more widely available than butter, making it a common kitchen staple.
Margarine’s higher smoke point helps the omelet stay golden longer without burning.
Traditionally the omelet was served with bread, fresh vegetables, or canned mushrooms.
Soviet cookbooks of the era often suggested a 1:1 substitution of butter with margarine.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain riboflavin (B2), cobalamin (B12) and folate, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of choline
items.content: Choline in the yolk is important for brain function and liver health.

items.title: Fatty acids
items.content: Margarine supplies necessary fatty acids, including omega‑6, which are building blocks of cell membranes.

items.title: Improved vitamin absorption
items.content: The fat from margarine aids the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K present in eggs.

items.title: Saturated and trans fats
items.content: Some margarines contain trans‑fatty acids and saturated fats that, when consumed in excess, may increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals with egg‑protein allergy can experience skin reactions or respiratory symptoms.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should monitor their intake.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Many margarines are salted; those watching sodium intake should choose unsalted varieties.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, either folded into a roll or cut into wedges. It pairs well with fresh vegetables, herbs, tomato sauce, or a light salad. Optional additions include cheese, ham, or chopped green onions for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Freshly cooked omelet is best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a little margarine to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts are a legume whose seeds are commonly called nuts. Roasted unsalted peanuts have a distinctive aroma, crunchy texture, and a mildly sweet flavor. They are eaten raw, roasted, and used in cooking, confectionery, sauces, and spreads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts belong to the legume family, not true nuts, although they are used like nuts in cuisine.
They originated in South America and were domesticated more than 3,500 years ago.
Peanut plants produce flowers that bend down to the ground, where they are fertilized and develop pods – the so‑called "groundnuts."
The United States produces over 30 % of the world’s peanuts, making it the largest producer.
Peanuts are used to make peanut butter, pastes, flour, and even peanut oil.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, providing a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: They are high in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts provide niacin, thiamine, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They supply magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, and iron, aiding muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Peanuts contain resveratrol and phenolic compounds that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common food allergens and can cause severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of their fat content, peanuts are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Aflatoxins
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth that produces aflatoxins; keep peanuts dry to avoid contamination.

items.title: Omega‑6 fatty acids
items.content: A high omega‑6 to omega‑3 ratio may promote inflammation if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peanuts can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, cereals, baked goods, sauces, and spreads. They are also processed into peanut butter and flour. Roasted unsalted peanuts are a versatile, health‑friendly option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peanuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard any nuts that smell rancid.

sausage-and-noodles-with-cream-or-white-.title: Sausage and noodles with cream or white sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Sausage and noodles with cream or white sauce (code 1311) is a ready‑to‑eat dish that combines boiled noodles, pieces of boiled or smoked sausage, and a smooth sauce made from cream or milk. It is popular in cafeterias and fast‑service restaurants as a quick lunch, providing a balanced mix of carbohydrates, protein and fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is often served in single‑serve plastic containers, making it easy to distribute in canteens.
The creamy sauce can be prepared with cream, milk, flour and spices, while the white sauce follows the classic béchamel recipe.
Noodles are usually short (such as “spaghetti” or “fettuccine”) and cooked al dente before mixing.
Sausage may be either boiled or smoked, influencing aroma and salt content.
The mild texture and neutral flavor make it a common choice for children’s meals.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Sausage provides quickly digestible protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbohydrates
items.content: Noodles supply glucose, helping maintain energy levels throughout the day.

items.title: Calcium from dairy sauce
items.content: The cream or white sauce, made with dairy, contributes calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sausage products are often enriched with B1, B2 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: The soft texture makes the dish suitable for people with chewing difficulties or for young children.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages can contain a lot of salt, which may raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cream‑based sauces and some sausages are rich in saturated fats, which should be limited in cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Ready‑made sausage may contain nitrites and other preservatives that should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Allergy risk
items.content: People allergic to dairy or specific meat proteins should avoid this dish.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, usually on a plate or in a tray. You can garnish with fresh vegetables, herbs or grated cheese for extra flavor. If desired, thin the sauce with a little milk to reduce richness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 1 month. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.
